newsitem.title: USA: Northern Plains flooding extends north into Canada.
newsitem.headline: Northern Plains flooding extends north into Canada.

text.p: The Red River, swollen with runoff from melting snow, inundated vast stretches of U.S. and Canadian prairie on Thursday as floodwaters slowly receded from devastated Grand Forks.

Manitoba issued an emergency evacuation order for 17,500 people in the Red River Valley, and hundreds of rural North Dakota residents fled their homes as the slow-moving crest gradually worked its way north toward Lake Winnipeg.
Three deaths this week in Manitoba have been blamed on the flooding.
Massive snowdrifts from a miserable winter continued to melt across the table-top prairie, sending sheets of water over farms and roads.
The battle against the rising river was being fought in small rural North Dakota towns of Drayton and Pembina, where people sandbagged through the night to protect emptied homes.

In Grand Forks, anxious residents called into a local radio station seeking word about whether the waters had ebbed in their neighbourhoods and to locate relatives who have scattered across the country.

Although 90 percent of the city of 50,000 remained under an evacuation order and there may be no clean water available for weeks, a few residents were back in dry areas cleaning up, using gas-powered pumps to drain fetid floodwaters from their basements. Officials warned of the dangers from uncertain electrical systems and contaminated water.
"People can't go in there because there's still safety and health hazards. It looks dry, but it's not safe," Grand Forks Mayor Pat Owens said.
Owens, who has expressed fears some residents would never return to the devastated city, said officials planned to divide the city into segments to organise and direct the cleanup effort.

The Red River fell to under 53 feet (16 metres) early on Thursday at Grand Forks, a foot lower than its crest earlier this week, leaving a slimy ring around buildings and trees. Some neighbourhoods were completely dry.
A week ago, the rampaging river surpassed National Weather Service predictions and swamped the cities of Grand Forks and East Grand Forks, Minnesota, a city of 9,500.
At the emergency shelter in an Air Force base 15 miles (24 km) west of Grand Forks, Frederick Fried, 82, pledged to return.
"My wife will go stay with her sister in Rhode Island, but I'll get in there and clean up," Fried said.
Some residents spoke not only of the displacement from homes but the loss of jobs when the flood and a subsequent fire devastated the downtown.

In Fargo, 75 miles (120 km) south and upstream from Grand Forks, where waters were receding, officials considered how to dismantle the huge diking system that kept much of the city dry. The sand from emptied sandbags may be used next on roads next winter or in construction projects.
